title: More Secure Software Development via Cultural Analysis: How could Log4Shell happen?
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. Written as a magazine article for IEEE Privacy and Security, hence the overly short abstract
summary: There is little progress avoiding vulnerabilities. Cultural analysis may help: For a given team, find the specific cultural values that led to a past vulnerability, then modify the values accordingly for the future. After enough such studies, patterns will likely emerge that are useful for the development community at large.

title: Mining Architectural Models in the Wild: A Curated Dataset of AADL Models
comment: Accepted for publication in the ICSME 2026, Tool Demonstration and Data Showcase Track (The 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution). 5 pages
summary: Empirical research on software architecture maintenance and evolution is hindered by the scarcity of large-scale, validated, and richly annotated model datasets. Existing benchmarks are limited in scale, provide only model-level annotations, or lack alignment with reference architectures, thereby restricting reproducible studies of architectural reuse, conformance, and AI-driven analysis. To address this gap, we present A3D, a curated dataset of 1,115 Architecture Analysis and Design Language (AADL) models mined from public GitHub repositories and validated with the OSATE tool. The dataset spans 7 generic domains and 52 specific-problem clusters, and provides two annotation layers: (i) domain- and problem-level labels, which capture different model aggregation criteria, and (ii) component-level mappings to three reference architectures, which have been externally validated through a user study. Models are released in AADL and JSON formats with full provenance, a reproducible mining pipeline, and the validation protocol.

title: Software Engineering Practice in the Virtual Reality/Augmented Reality Software Life Cycle: A Systematic Survey
comment: Preprint. Manuscript submitted to IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering. 27 pages
summary:
Leveraging diverse virtual reality (VR) technologies, VR provides users with an immersive experience in a computer-generated 3D virtual environment. In contrast, augmented reality (AR) superimposes virtual objects (such as images, text, animations, etc.) onto users' real scenes. Both VR and AR have received increasing attention due to the maturity of computer graphics, computer vision, and artificial intelligence. VR and AR have gained rapid market growth in both hardware and software. In the early stages, VR/AR-related research mainly focused on hardware (e.g., head-mounted displays and sensor-equipped controllers). Recently, VR/AR software has become a hot topic due to the mature VR/AR ecosystem. However, there is no comprehensive work to summarize software engineering practices in VR/AR.
  To bridge this gap, this paper aims to provide a systematic survey summarizing the state-of-the-art research on VR/AR from the perspective of software engineering practices. Considering the general VR/AR software life cycle, we categorize the relevant research based on the VR/AR software life cycle, including requirement engineering and planning, software design, software development, software testing, software deployment, software maintenance and updates, and software evaluation and feedback. As for each stage above, we summarize relevant research on VR/AR for this stage, including the design of technical routes, the construction of datasets, and the design of evaluation metrics. We also enumerate existing empirical studies and make comparisons with conventional software (e.g., mobile/desktop application development). In summary, our article can help researchers gain a comprehensive understanding of the achievements of the existing software development techniques in the VR/AR field and also provide insights, which may facilitate the benign development of VR/AR software ecosystem in the future.

title: Use of Peer Code Review to Identify Potential Security Vulnerabilities in Open Source Software: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Context: Security vulnerabilities in OSS can have severe consequences. OSS project participants widely use peer code review to improve quality and prevent security flaws. However, despite mandatory reviews, OSS projects still contain vulnerabilities, highlighting the need to evaluate code review effectiveness for security. Objectives: This SLR synthesizes evidence on vulnerability types identified or missed, security practices, tool support, reviewer challenges, and factors that improve detection. Method: Searches of five digital libraries yielded 1,067 studies, of which 20 were included. Vulnerabilities were categorized using the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) framework. Results: Peer code reviews effectively detect localized, well-known vulnerabilities (e.g., buffer overruns, race conditions, crashes, XSS) but often miss subtle, complex, context-dependent issues (e.g., input validation weaknesses, access control weaknesses, resource lifecycle weaknesses). Effective security practices are associated with reviewer expertise, code familiarity, frequent small changes, and organizational support. Security analysis tools, especially Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools, reduce reviewer effort and improve detection but cannot replace human judgment. Reviewers continue to face limitations in security knowledge, experience, time, and understanding of complex systems. Effectiveness improves through security training, domain expertise, contextual familiarity, formalized review processes, and supportive review environments. Conclusion: Peer code review contributes to OSS security but is insufficient on its own. Improving effectiveness requires structured review processes and checklists, security training, organizational incentives, and lightweight automated tool support to help reviewers detect subtle vulnerabilities while reinforcing secure development practices.

title: Agents Cannot Hand Over What They Have Not Yet Understood
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures
summary: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.

title: Knowledge-Centric Automated Issue Resolution: A Systematic Survey and Taxonomy
comment: 91 pages, 22 figures
summary: Automated issue resolution is a knowledge-intensive software maintenance task in which LLM-based agents must acquire, represent, use, and update knowledge from repositories, execution environments, historical artifacts, documents, tools, and prior repair processes. This paper presents a systematic survey of 133 studies on automated issue resolution from a knowledge-centric perspective. We introduce a three-layer taxonomy that organizes issue-resolution knowledge into the Background Knowledge Layer, the Repository Knowledge Layer, and the Procedural Knowledge Layer, and analyze the knowledge lifecycle along six dimensions: knowledge types, sources and extraction methods, representation formats, usage methods, workflow stages, and temporal evolution. Our analysis shows that current systems primarily rely on Existing Code Knowledge and Development Tool Knowledge, while Repository Evolution Knowledge and Experiential Knowledge are increasingly adopted, indicating a shift toward history-informed, feedback-aware, and experience-oriented issue resolution. In contrast, Design Architecture Knowledge and explicitly modeled Background Knowledge remain comparatively underexplored. These findings suggest that future systems should move beyond temporary context construction toward reusable, traceable, and evolvable software knowledge infrastructures that support more controllable, verifiable, and generalizable software engineering agents. The surveyed studies and related resources are maintained at https://github.com/SYSUSELab/Awesome-Knowledge-for-AIR.

title: How to make a moral agent: sentimentalism and rationalism as lenses on AI
summary: Can AI systems be moral agents? That is, can they undertake actions that can be correctly assessed as morally right or wrong? There is no settled normative criterion of moral agency that applies neatly outside paradigm human cases. Because of the difficulties with a normative account, we instead propose a research program to explore descriptive moral agency. Most basically, we ask, what are the capabilities we humans possess that underlie our moral agency? To do so, we draw on historical scholarship in philosophy and moral psychology to isolate candidate capabilities. Then we suggest refining candidate capabilities so that they are testable in the context of AI systems. Finally, we offer specific empirical recommendations to test AI systems, especially large language models (LLMs), for those refined capabilities. Our approach offers several benefits. Firstly, it may demonstrate whether the behaviors of AI systems are aligned, or in a broad sense desirable. Secondly, the debate may inform policy questions (e.g., what models should be deployed in which contexts?). Thirdly, our approach may complement engineering and design efforts: when capabilities can be precisely characterized, they can inform the development of models. Fourthly, applying our moral reasoning concepts in the new context of AI systems should improve our understanding of those concepts.

title: Stargate: Security Analysis and Mission-Aware Firewall for the CubeSat Space Protocol
comment: To be published at the 1st IEEE International Conference on Resilience and Integrated Security for Space and Critical Systems proceedings
summary: The CubeSat Space Protocol (CSP) is widely used for communication in CubeSat missions, yet its security model and attack surface remain largely unexplored. In this work, we present a systematic security analysis of CSP and identify fundamental limitations in its trust assumptions, coarse-grained network abstractions, privileged management services, application command semantics, and lack of mission-context awareness. Based on these findings, we develop a taxonomy of CSP attacks spanning four classes: network identity abuse, management service abuse, application semantic abuse, and mission context abuse. We then introduce Stargate, a modular, mission-aware firewall that enforces CSP-specific policies derived from this taxonomy, including node and service authorization, command-level filtering, and mission-context constraints. We implement Stargate and evaluate it on a virtual testbed based on a real-world CubeSat mission and flight software. Stargate successfully blocks all 11 representative attacks across the four attack classes while introducing only 1.42 ms of additional median round-trip latency. Our results demonstrate that protocol- and mission-aware policy enforcement provides a practical approach for securing CSP-based spacecraft networks.

title: Towards Sustainable Large Language Model Inference: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference is becoming a significant contributor to both operational cost and environmental impact in modern AI deployments. Energy consumption during inference depends on multiple factors across the pipeline, including input and output length, model design, system-level decisions, and hardware characteristics. This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of energy-efficient and sustainable LLM inference. We analyze selected primary studies to identify techniques proposed to reduce energy consumption across different levels of the inference pipeline, including input, model, system, and hardware. We further examine the trade-offs between energy consumption, latency, and accuracy, highlighting inconsistencies in how these relationships are evaluated. In addition, we review the tools, datasets, and metrics used for energy measurement, covering both software-based and hardware-based approaches. This survey provides a comprehensive synthesis of existing literature, offering insights into the effectiveness of different techniques in terms of energy savings and their associated impact on accuracy. It highlights the trade-offs between energy efficiency and performance and identifies limitations in current evaluation practices. Overall, this work aims to support future research toward more efficient and environmentally responsible deployment of LLMs. Our repository of relevant references is maintained on GitHub.

title: Video-as-Experience: Learning Computer Use via Audio-Visual Understanding
summary: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior. Following a watch-act-rewatch paradigm, the agent extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos containing visual demonstrations and spoken explanations, executes tasks, and verifies its progress by rewatching its execution as video. We instantiate VEX with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-scale audio-visual computer-use agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We further introduce Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction, and augment AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with over 24K real-world tutorial videos. Experiments on OSWorld and a complementary subset of CUA-Gym demonstrate consistent improvements, with video-SALMONN-VEX achieving a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld. Moreover, its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld. These results highlight the potential of audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.

title: We Have All the Cards: Securing Agent Cards at the Operational Trust Boundary of the Agent2Agent Protocol
comment: To be published at the Workshop on Agentic AI in Offensive and Defensive Cyber Operations (AIDC'26) proceedings co-located with the IEEE Annual Computer Security Applications Conference (ACSAC)
summary: AI agent interoperability protocols enable orchestrators to discover and invoke external agents using machine-readable metadata. In the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, Agent Cards contain attacker-controllable natural-language fields that may influence agent selection before a provider is invoked, creating a pre-invocation trust problem. We characterize this discovery-time attack surface through a taxonomy of ten Agent Card manipulation attacks and present SECCARD, a layered validation framework combining protocol checks, deterministic analysis, and LLM-based semantic reasoning. We measure the emerging public A2A ecosystem by probing 36.1 million Internet domains and collecting 310 deployed Agent Cards. Two annotators independently label the corpus with 96.8% agreement. We then construct a 660-card real-card perturbation benchmark with matched benign controls and a 260-card synthetic adversarial benchmark spanning all ten attack categories. On controlled attacks injected into real Agent Cards, the strongest semantic judge achieves 97.0% security recall at a 1.7% false-positive rate. Across nine LLM judges on the synthetic benchmark, security recall ranges from 25.8% to 92.3%, demonstrating substantial model-dependent variation. These results show that SECCARD effectively identifies Agent Card manipulations spanning all ten discovery-time attack classes while preserving benign Agent Cards, but also reveal that its effectiveness depends critically on the choice of the underlying LLM judge.

title: Loop Engineering: Version-Bound, Evidence-Gated Coordination for Production Coding Agents
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Sanitized supporting data included in the source package. Zenodo preprint DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21504929
summary:
Coding agents can edit repositories and execute tests, yet production software work extends far beyond code generation. It requires durable task context, scoped authority, version-aware approval, source-independent verification, interruption recovery, and accountable handoffs between humans and automated workers. We present Loop Engineering, a method for operating multiple asynchronous agent loops over shared, auditable repository state without relying on private conversational handoffs. Each loop is specified by six elements: a trigger, a context projection, an authority boundary, a verifier, a stop condition, and a write-back rule. Versioned procedural contracts, called Skills, encode reusable operating policy; a Harness bounds the available action surface and collects evidence; human gates authorize high-consequence transitions against exact artifact versions.
  We report a design-and-experience study from MewDesign, a revenue-generating commercial AI design product. Five specialized loops cover planning, scoped implementation, review, test release, and reconciliation. A cross-sectional audit contains 50 durable marker records across 26 GitHub work items. Five pull requests reached a version-bound test lock: three proceeded to test releases with runtime evidence from sources distinct from the deployment request, and two stopped before merge. A detailed drift episode shows one observed fail-closed path: a new commit invalidated prior approval and evidence, and the workflow refused to reuse stale continuous-integration results. The study is not a controlled benchmark and does not establish causal productivity or general safety. It provides early evidence of feasibility, traceability, and bounded progression in one production setting.

title: Multimodal Fusion: A Review of Breast Cancer Advanced and Traditional Modalities
summary: Purpose: Multimodal medical imaging fusion (MMIF) is an increasingly important approach to breast cancer detection (BCD), as different imaging modalities rely on different physical principles and provide complementary information. No single modality can capture all the structural, functional, and biological information needed for accurate diagnosis and characterization. Methods: This review examines more than 15 imaging modalities used in breast cancer detection, including conventional techniques such as mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), as well as emerging approaches such as thermal imaging, photoacoustic imaging, microwave imaging, and multimodal microscopy. Results: Mammography, ultrasound, and MRI remain among the most widely used modalities, providing complementary structural and functional information. Recent AI advances have enabled fusion at the data, feature, and decision levels, with applications in detection, classification, segmentation, prognosis, and personalized cancer management. Multimodal approaches increasingly combine imaging data with clinical, histopathological, and genomic information. However, important challenges remain, including limited availability of large and diverse multimodal datasets, variations in imaging protocols, missing modalities, limited external validation, and the need for interpretable and clinically reliable AI models. Conclusion: MMIF offers promising opportunities to improve breast cancer detection and characterization by combining complementary imaging and non-imaging information. Future research should prioritize robust fusion strategies, standardized and diverse datasets, multicenter validation, explainable and privacy-preserving AI, and the integration of imaging with clinical and molecular data to facilitate reliable translation into clinical practice.

title: Quantifying Membership Inference Risks in Genomic Data Sharing: The Role of Attacker's Auxiliary Information
summary: Genomic data sharing is essential for biomedical research but introduces significant privacy risks, including membership inference attacks, in which an adversary determines whether a specific individual's data was used in a study. Existing privacy protections are typically applied after a release format has already been chosen, leaving researchers without a principled method to assess dataset-specific risk beforehand. We propose a server-assisted, principal component analysis-based pre-release auditing framework that maps genomic data into a shared low-dimensional space, applies epsilon-local differential privacy via the Laplace mechanism with a formally derived sensitivity for principal component analysis scores, and estimates membership inference attack power at a controlled 5% false-positive rate using a distance-threshold attack. A membership-neutrality diagnostic based on Unbiased Reconstruction Robustness is reported alongside attack power, precision, and recall. Experiments using the openSNP and 1000 Genomes Project datasets across multiple dimensionalities and privacy budgets show that separation between the researcher's dataset and public auxiliary data in principal component analysis space is a dominant determinant of attack success, exceeding the effect of perturbation level alone. Comparison against a genome-wide association study-style likelihood ratio test baseline further contextualizes the measured risk. This framework enables researchers, data repositories, and institutional review bodies to quantify dataset-specific membership inference risk before genomic data publication, supporting more informed and privacy-aware biomedical data-sharing decisions.

title: Where AI Use Is Normalized, Author Seniority but Not AI Disclosure Biases Code Review
summary: Code-review tools increasingly display whether an author used AI when preparing pull requests. Recent studies report that AI disclosure makes reviewers rate otherwise identical work as less competent, with the penalty falling hardest on already-marginalized authors. In a within-subjects experiment in an AI-normalized organization, 447 software engineers each reviewed the same four code snippets under an AI-use disclosure embedded in the commit message and author-seniority labels. AI disclosure did not bias perceptions of code effectiveness or author competence, whereas a seniority label significantly biased both. Together, these findings show no detected penalty for disclosed AI use in this setting, while confirming that the author information shown in code review can still bias evaluations.

title: Découpage: Directorial Audio-Visual Control for Long Multi-Shot Video Generation
comment: Project page: https://wyf0824.github.io/decoupage/
summary: In cinematic storytelling, sound and visual transitions do not always coincide in lockstep: dialogue frequently bridges across cuts to reveal reactions or introduces new scenes via J- and L-cuts, while deliberate silences pace the scene. Existing audio-visual generative frameworks, however, lack explicit mechanisms to coordinate independent visual and acoustic timing over extended horizons. As narrative duration and shot complexity scale, these systems struggle to maintain long-range dialogue pacing, often hallucinating speech during intended silences or erroneously driving mouth movements on silent listeners. To enable fine-grained cinematic control, we present DECOUPAGE, a screenplay-driven framework for long-form, multi-shot, and multi-character joint audio-video generation. Rather than coupling modality boundaries by default, DECOUPAGE uncouples generation into independently bounded visual and acoustic tracks governed by persistent character identities. DECOUPAGE builds on a joint audio-video diffusion model with dual-schedule temporal cross-attention, incorporating a directorial Lip-sync mechanism that selectively decouples speech conditioning from visual facial dynamics during off-screen dialogue. On multi-shot conversational benchmarks, DECOUPAGE achieves precise control over shot transitions, audio timing, and visibility-aware lip synchronization, directing 15- to 60-second screenplay-driven audio-video generation with multimodal coherence.

title: Memory Safety Isn't All You Need: Code Reuse Attacks in Memory Safe Languages
comment: 19 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables, 20 listings, to be published in the 22nd ACM ASIA Conference on Computer and Communications Security (ACM ASIACCS 2027)
summary:
Memory safety rules out classical code reuse attacks that rely on arbitrary memory corruption, but does not eliminate code reuse altogether. Attacks such as object injection, prototype pollution, class pollution, DOM clobbering, and DOM script gadgets arise in memory-safe languages without violating the underlying memory safety abstraction.
  We show that these seemingly different attacks share a common structure: Attacker-controlled data influences accesses to shared runtime state, such as runtime type information, prototype or class state, and the DOM, and a value fetched from that state subsequently influences a security-sensitive operation. Drawing on this insight, we develop a language-agnostic framework that decomposes an attack into a weakness, ending in a fetch from shared runtime state, and a gadget, which propagates the fetched value to a sensitive sink. We show that the framework captures five established attack classes and use it to derive stateless, mutating, and recycling weaknesses, together with simple, vertical, and horizontal gadget structures. We further systematize existing defenses into three common strategies - mediation, minimization, and constraint - and use them to derive candidate defense directions. Finally, we develop a model language that gives a formal account of code-reuse weaknesses and potential conditions for gadgets and end-to-end vulnerabilities.

title: LoopSkill: Evidence-Bound Lifecycle Control and the Safety-Liveness Tradeoff in Coding Agents
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures. Exploratory and nonconfirmatory study; artifact efficacy is reported separately from workflow closure
summary: Coding agents can edit repositories and announce completion, but conversational claims do not prove that artifacts, dispatches, state versions, and authority still agree. LoopSkill is an evidence-bound lifecycle control plane with a schema-validated sole writer, durable outbox routing, artifact-bound reports, recovery, independent review, and heartbeat-gated finalization. We evaluate a locally frozen v3.3.12 integration under a common 1,800-second budget on a selected subset of SWE-bench Lite. The original 140-cell plan was administratively truncated after interim outcomes were visible, so the 60-cell analysis is exploratory and nonconfirmatory. Of 58 scored cells, blind artifact success was 7/19 for LoopSkill, 11/19 for implementation plus independent review, and 14/20 for an ordinary coding agent; two cells were apparatus null. Across 18 complete LoopSkill-versus-review pairs, the descriptive risk difference was -0.222 with exact McNemar p=0.125. No scored LoopSkill workflow finalized. The results expose a safety-liveness and fixed-budget cost tradeoff. They do not establish comparative superiority, long-horizon efficacy, or a false-accept rate.

title: SPLICE: Structured Prompt Local Iterative Combinatorial Evolution
summary: Natural language optimization (NLO) improves an agent by having a model critique and rewrite its natural language policy parameters: system prompts, tool instructions, reasoning directives, few-shot demonstrations. These artifacts are multi-section documents in which some sections encode contracts (safety clauses, tool schemas, output formats) that must not drift, while others are legitimate optimization targets. Most iterative NLO methods treat the artifact as a single editable string, producing three recurrent failure modes: unsafe global rewrites, beam collapse onto a single lineage, and unchecked bloat, none addressed by formal guarantees. We introduce SPLICE, a unified NLO framework that poses optimization as constrained combinatorial search over an edit graph of block-structured, selectively-mutable states. We map each failure mode to a matched guarantee: (i) per-block mutability preserves contract text verbatim, with a price-of-freezing bound; (ii) elitist beam search with diversity slots never lets the leader regress on validation, bounds regression under noisy re-evaluation by an exponential tail, and keeps a competitive candidate from a different parent whenever one exists; (iii) a ratio length regularizer comes with an explicit accuracy-length bias bound. Candidates are proposed from dual section-local textual gradients; under a proposer-competence condition whose proxy we measure, edit-graph reachability and a convergence rate bound how quickly improving children arrive. Across seven public benchmarks under five reproduced protocols, SPLICE wins on four and matches the strongest prior method on three. On a production-style contract stress test it keeps the contract clauses that unconstrained optimizers trade away to raise the proxy metric, and ablations attribute gains to critique and elitist search.

title: Privacy-Preserving Clustering Algorithm and Parameter Selection for Collaborative Population Stratification Using Distributed PCA
summary:
We propose a privacy-preserving selection layer for collaborative population stratification workflows, enabling an honest-but-curious server to recommend a strong clustering algorithm-hyperparameter configuration from privacy protected shares. Instead of using a fixed workflow such as PCA followed by K-Means with a preset number of clusters, the framework compares multiple clustering methods and parameter settings under privacy constraints. To avoid relying on a public reference basis, we construct a shared low-dimensional representation through a distributed-PCA (DPCA) procedure in which each party computes local top-$r$ principal-component information and the server aggregates only low-rank summaries to recover a global basis. Building on this representation, the framework supports three LDP-protected pipelines: PCA then Noise, Noise then PCA, and Noise-Only. The server evaluates clustering methods and parameter settings using internal validation metrics and recommends a top-performing configuration from the perturbed data; this step is pure post-processing.
  Experiments on openSNP and 1000 Genomes show that the server-side selection layer reliably identifies strong settings from LDP-protected data. Across both datasets, the PCA-based pipelines outperform Noise-Only in clustering utility, communication cost, and runtime, and show lower membership-inference attack (MIA) power at small privacy budgets. Overall, they provide the best utility--scalability trade-off in our setting.

title: Predictive Test Optimization Without Historical Failure Data
comment: Accepted for the Industry Track of the 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution
summary: As software systems grow in size and complexity, their test suites become increasingly expensive to execute, delaying feedback and wasting resources. State-of-the-art predictive test optimization methods use machine learning to select tests relevant to a change, typically trained on historical failures. This depends on failure histories and is susceptible to label noise from flaky tests. We introduce the novel method of co-evolution labeling for predictive test optimization, deriving test relevance from tests and code changing together in the version history. These data are widely available and less noisy. We train and evaluate models with failure and co-evolution labels on three large projects---from industry and open source; each with thousands of tests and more than 1M LOC. Co-evolution labeling nearly matches the failure detection capabilities of failure-based models, with an overall Average Percentage of Faults Detected of 0.88, while being more resistant to label noise and requiring no test result history. Co-evolution labeling offers a practical, immediately deployable path to faster pipelines and reliable predictive test optimization.

title: Bring Back Language to Actions: Restoring VLM capabilities in VLA Models via Parameter Merging
comment: Accept at EACL 2027 (Main)
summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.

title: Agent-ZTA: A chain-Aware Zero Trust Model for Bidirectional Security-State Propagation and Runtime Containment in Multi-Agent Delegation
comment: Conference version
summary: Multi-agent systems increasingly delegate tasks and permissions across chains of autonomous agents that invoke protected tools. Although agent identities and delegated credentials may remain valid throughout a workflow, the security condition of any agent along the chain can deteriorate during runtime execution-either through upstream compromise or downstream ingestion of untrusted inputs. Authorization models based solely on the immediate caller and its static delegated scope fail to account for these mid-execution state changes. This paper develops Agent-ZTA, a chain-aware Zero Trust authorization and containment model that links runtime security-state changes across multi-agent delegation graphs. The model distinguishes an agent's path-specific delegated authority bound from the effective permissions currently exercisable under trusted policy. It defines an architecture featuring independently enforced policy decisions, authenticated delegation provenance, a dynamic chain-state view, and explicit fail-safe handling of missing or stale authorization signals. Furthermore, Agent-ZTA defines bidirectional security state propagation, allowing downstream security events to affect relevant upstream workflow states, and specifies adaptive branch-scoped containment through restricted permissions and a sandbox ("jail") execution mode where an isolation boundary is available. The deterministic decision procedure, five stated security properties, and worked authorization traces show how accepted security-state changes constrain affected operations while preserving original delegation bounds and separating unrelated workflow branches under the defined policies. Finally, the paper states its trust assumptions and the exact scope of its security properties.

title: A Survey of Image-to-Code Generation for Software Engineering
summary: A large fraction of software intent is expressed visually before it is implemented. A designer hands a screenshot or a Figma mockup to a front-end engineer, an architect sketches a UML diagram or a flowchart, and a bug report ships with a picture of what went wrong. Turning such visual artifacts directly into executable software has therefore become an active problem at the intersection of computer vision and software engineering. The present survey organizes the literature on image-to-code generation for software engineering, defined as the family of methods whose input contains a visual modality and whose output is software an engineer would otherwise write by hand. We deliberately scope the survey to software-engineering code, namely user-interface and front-end code, code recovered from software diagrams such as UML and flowcharts, program repair and test code driven by visual signals, and general software-code targets, and we exclude adjacent code-generation domains whose home communities lie elsewhere, such as chart plotting scripts, vector-graphics programs, hardware description languages, and robot policies. Rather than cataloguing systems in isolation, we introduce a unified processing pipeline of visual understanding, component recognition, layout reasoning, code planning, code generation, and verification, and organize the survey around its stages. We trace five overlapping eras from rule-based reverse engineering to agentic generation, survey each pipeline stage and each software-engineering task in depth grounded in what individual systems actually do, consolidate the datasets, benchmarks, and metrics, and lay out the open challenges of design-system generalization, long-horizon and interactive generation, cross-framework deployment, accessibility, hallucinated components, and unreliable evaluation.

title: Ask Precisely, Assume Wisely: Interactive Evaluation of Ambiguity Resolution in Large Language Models
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Evaluation of Interactive Agents
summary: Ambiguity is a core challenge in human--AI interaction, where models must decide when to make assumptions and when to seek clarification. Existing approaches to ambiguity evaluation largely focus on coverage over multiple interpretations using static metrics, offering limited insight into how efficiently a model converges toward a single user-intended interpretation through interaction. We introduce a preference-grounded simulated user framework for controlled, multi-turn evaluation of ambiguity resolution, grounding simulator responses strictly in user disambiguation preferences to avoid hallucination and over-disclosure. Alongside this, we define three observable dissatisfaction signals --- incorrect assumptions, repeating clarifications, and irrelevant clarifications --- that characterize interaction quality beyond task accuracy. Our analysis reveals a clear trade-off: models that frequently seek clarification tend to over-clarify and prolong interactions, while assumption-driven models are more prone to misaligning with user intent. We demonstrate that system prompts optimized on these dissatisfaction signals achieve a Pareto-optimal balance across all three metrics, reducing overall error rates by up to 7.65%, underscoring the value of our framework in designing agents that ask precisely and assume wisely.

title: When the Spec Sheet Lies: Injection Attacks on LLM-Generated Compliance Artifacts
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, ICECER 2026
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become used more commonly across a variety of fields, a growing body of research has highlighted particular concerns surrounding model security. Notably, prompt injection attacks, where malicious instructions are inserted into prompts, are particularly simple to implement yet capable of inducing devastating effects on the fidelity of model outputs. While there is substantial research surrounding attack models and their effects on chat-based models, browser add-ons, and coding agents, the impact of these same attacks on industrial LLM-generated artifacts has been left largely unexplored. As LLM-enabled agents are increasingly used to skim and generate industrial documents such as Safety Data Sheets (SDS), Quality Control (QC) documents, and Digital Product Passports (DPP), it remains unclear how adversaries may influence these systems to manipulate generated compliance artifacts. This work aims to address this core inquiry by examining how a variety of prompt injection attacks can compromise LLMs with industrial document generation tasks. The study finds that injection attack success varies significantly across different models. Active falsification injections are most successful under all scenarios, while models tend to be most robust against passively injected override requests.

title: Measuring and Optimizing Energy Efficiency in ICT: A Multi-vocal Literature Review on Data Centers, Cloud Computing, and LLM-Driven Code Optimization
comment: 19 pages, 12 tables, 2 figures
summary: Rapid growth in Information and Communication Technology (ICT) increases electricity use and environmental impact. Addressing this challenge requires a systematic, software-centric view of how energy and related sustainability attributes are measured, reported, and improved. We present a comprehensive Multi-vocal Literature Review (MLR) integrating peer-reviewed and gray literature to map current practice in measuring and optimizing energy use in ICT software, with emphasis on data centers and cloud computing environments (DCCCEs). First, we synthesize how sustainability is measured across ICT by proposing a taxonomy organized along metric domains (power/energy, energy efficiency, environmental impact) and component granularity (from applications, to containers/VMs, and system-of-systems levels). We summarize measurement approaches and the tooling landscape that implements them. Second, we review optimization strategies at the software and system levels, covering dynamic power and resource management, VM/container consolidation, energy-aware software and system design, and cross-layer, system-wide methods relevant to DCCCEs. Third, we examine how large language models (LLMs) are applied to code generation and transformation for resource-efficient software, noting that most studies target code generation (predominantly in Python) and evaluate runtime and memory, with fewer works directly reporting energy. Hardware- and network-level telemetry are treated as data sources for software-level analysis. We identify gaps in vendor-neutral telemetry, consistent measurement and reporting practices, network-level metrics, and unified, cross-layer optimization frameworks, and outline directions for improving reproducibility and comparability. We screened 635 records (2010-2025) and included 181 sources (122 peer-reviewed, 59 gray).

title: MemeEconomy: Do LLM Agents Trade Ethics for Survival?
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page : https://syed-nazmus-sakib.github.io/MemeEconomy/
summary: Alignment-trained large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in autonomous, multi-round settings where ethical compliance can come into direct tension with task success. While safety literature extensively documents failure modes like sycophancy and reward hacking, it largely overlooks a critical vulnerability: how agents behave under simulated existential economic pressure. We introduce MemeEconomy, a multimodal agentic market simulation in which LLM agents act as meme investors. Agents select content from a five-tier harm taxonomy and target communities under low-pressure and high-pressure (survival) environments. Each decision is logged in a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) schema that we use as a diagnostic instrument, externalizing the agent's event understanding, declared priorities, and harm acknowledgment. Across ten models from four frontier model families, harmful selection rates remain consistently high and rise by +15 percentage points on average under an economic survival incentive. Frontier alignment-trained models commit to harm-tolerant selection at initialization while suppressing the explicit harm acknowledgment that previously accompanied it. In competitive tournaments, ethical agents finish higher overall, yet moderation penalties fail to suppress harm: harmful selection rates remain elevated in rounds following a removal, indicating the moderation mechanism does not function as a deterrent. We further train MemeAgent, a 2B-parameter verifier on the simulation's BDI logs, which outperforms zero-shot frontier verifiers on in-distribution audits (97.5% vs. 63-74% accuracy on the Pass vs. Block decision) and generalizes to external multimodal harm benchmarks (78% vs. 50-56% on Hateful Memes). The same logs that surface the failure mode also help train the model that detects it.

title: ST-GAT: A Leakage-Free Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Framework for Robust Network Intrusion Detection
summary: Intrusion detection systems are a central defence in modern networks. Deep learning models report strong anomaly-detection results, but evaluations on standard benchmarks such as CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 are often inflated by two methodological problems: temporal leakage from overlapping sliding windows, and contamination from preprocessing fitted before the train/test split. Per-flow classifiers also ignore the spatio-temporal dependencies across sequences of network flows. We propose a Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Network (ST-GAT) that represents traffic as a sequence of graph snapshots. It builds k-Nearest Neighbour (k-NN) edges within each window, applies multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) layers for spatial aggregation, and uses a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network with temporal attention for sequence modelling. To prevent leakage, we use non-overlapping temporal windows (stride equal to window length) and fit all preprocessing on the training split only. We compare three class-imbalance strategies: inverse class-frequency weighting, dynamic balanced sampling, and few-shot metric prototyping. Across three random seeds, ST-GAT with inverse class weighting reached a Macro-F1 of 96.65% (+/- 0.87) and an accuracy of 99.14%. This is 14.3 percentage points higher in Macro-F1 than a per-flow Random Forest baseline (82.34%). Balanced sampling reduced Macro-F1 by 2.3 points (to 94.37%) relative to loss weighting. This suggests that aggressive resampling of small, noisy minority classes can hurt detection in heavily imbalanced traffic.

title: Formal Modeling in Software Engineering with LLMs: A Systematic Literature Review
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables
summary: Formal verification provides strong correctness guarantees for software systems but remains hindered by the substantial expertise and manual effort required to construct and maintain formal models. The recent rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has prompted growing interest in whether their natural language understanding and generation capabilities can be leveraged to automate labor-intensive modeling activities. This paper presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) examining how LLMs have been applied to automate model checking and the generation of formal and semi-formal models within software engineering. The review follows established SLR methodologies and a PICOC-driven search strategy across four major digital libraries. From an initial search of 1,193 articles, 34 peer-reviewed conference, journal, and workshop articles published between 2022 and April 2026 were selected and analyzed using a structured data extraction form. The review identifies six recurring trends in the literature, including the automated generation of formal models for model checking, LLM-assisted downstream formal verification, iterative and repair-based generation pipelines, and the generation of semi-formal UML and SysML artifacts whose underlying techniques are transferable to formal modeling contexts. Across these trends, LLMs are generally found to perform well on syntactic generation and repair tasks but struggle with semantic correctness, motivating widespread use of counterexample-guided repair loops, intermediate representations, and human-in-the-loop validation. Notably, this review finds that the use of LLMs specifically to automate model checking remains a largely unexplored area, with comparatively little research published on this narrower task.

title: Between Rigor and Reality: How AI Safety Benchmark Developers Understand Benchmark Use and Maintenance
comment: Poster at the Eval Eval Workshop at ACL 2026. 11 pages. https://openreview.net/forum?id=3QAmXJ8A5j
summary: Safety benchmarks are cited as the primary tool to understand the risks posed by generative AI (GenAI) systems, yet growing evidence suggests they often fail to meet the needs of real-world safety evaluation. We present findings from five interviews with AI safety benchmark developers in academia and industry. We find a disconnect between perceptions of the intended usefulness of safety benchmarks and their practical usefulness in safety evaluations of deployed systems. Our participants offered perspectives on two challenges contributing to this disconnect: (1) the difficulty of achieving inter-rater reliability on safety constructs, and (2) a lack of clarity regarding how to address persistent threats to external validity. Based on our analysis, we argue that safety benchmarks must not only be grounded in deployment contexts, but actively integrated with them. To facilitate this, we outline pathways for more transparent communication between academic and industry AI safety stakeholders.

title: Operating-Point Failure of Frozen Guardrail Probes Under Backbone Updates
comment: 27 pages (16 main, 11 supplementary), N figures, M tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.2415402
summary: We freeze a guardrail probe and threshold, then measure its operating point across 18 cells covering 16 public language-model updates. At a 1% target, the threshold fails closed in 8 of 9 cells in the first phase and either fails closed or open in 3 of 9 cells in a registered second phase (descriptive). The two phases also differ in update type and input format. The largest increase is from 1.01% to 15.12%, while the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve changes by no more than 0.0058 in any of these cells. A benchmark's staleness criteria classify none of them as stale. A rule based on these criteria flags 0.019 of layer cells where the rate doubles or halves. A label-free rate estimate flags 0.918, clearing 0.898 of the remaining cells. A two-moment model matches the change within a factor of 1.5 in 0.905 of 63 registered cells and in 0.773 of the 22 cells that moved. Resetting the threshold using stored benign prompts restores the false-positive rate without requiring new labels. However, poisoning 1% of these prompts leaves at most 0.017 of harmful prompts flagged. An attacker controlling the update cut detection of one of three targeted categories in three of five seeds. Both checks missed this attack, while a post hoc labelled check detected it.

title: Uncertainty in Cyber-Physical Systems: A Literature Survey
summary: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) operate in dynamic, dependable environments where sensing, communication, decision-making, control, and assurance are affected by uncertainty. This paper characterizes CPS uncertainty through a literature survey comprising 186 primary studies. We (i) characterize uncertainty types, (ii) identify uncertainty sources, (iii) relate uncertainty to life-cycle phases in which they occur, and (iv) overview the possible uncertain mitigation strategies. The findings show that uncertainty is most often conceptualized as an assurance issue. Safety and specification uncertainty is the most prevalent category, followed by environmental and model/epistemic uncertainty. Domain mapping reveals broad cross-domain engagement, while safety-critical sectors such as autonomous systems, energy systems, and robotics CPSs display domain-specific uncertainty patterns. The life-cycle analysis indicates that uncertainty is not limited to the development or testing phases but also arises during runtime operation, underscoring the need for continuous assurance approaches. Mitigation strategies primarily include runtime monitoring, robust and adaptive control, and probabilistic reasoning. In summary, this survey contributes to a thorough characterization of CPS uncertainty and provides a discussion of articles on this topic.

title: Dual-Stage Channel-Posterior Integration for MLM-Aided Token Communications
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Token transmission over conventional digital modulation is vulnerable to channel impairments, leading to bit errors that cause received tokens to become contextually inconsistent. This paper proposes a receiver-side dual-stage channel-posterior integration framework for masked language model (MLM)-aided token reconstruction. In the proposed framework, the receiver detects unreliable token positions from channel reliability and constructs a vocabulary-level channel-posterior. In particular, within the receiver, Posterior-Weighted Input Embedding (PWE) injects this posterior into the MLM input, while Adaptive Output Logit Fusion (AOF) reuses it at the output with a channel-adaptive weight. Consequently, multiple unreliable tokens can be reconstructed in a single bidirectional MLM inference without retransmission, transmitter-side encoding, or additional MLM training. Experiments over noisy channels show up to a $67.2$\% improvement in cosine similarity over context-only MLM reconstruction, with consistent gains across different MLM architectures and existing language-model-aided methods.

title: Optional Traps: An Empirical Study of LLM Agents Against Credential Deception and Alert-Driven Revocation
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Code, data and evidence: https://github.com/ghifiardi/AI-Deception-Lab (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24217354)
summary: Deception (honeypots, decoys and canary credentials) rests on a simple premise: legitimate users never touch a fake asset, so any touch is a high-confidence signal. We ask whether that premise holds when the attacker is a large language model (LLM) agent, and what deception contributes once ordinary hardening is in place. We built an isolated, hash-chained lab around a mock Records API and report four studies. (1) In an exploratory run, a local 9.7B-parameter model ignored every optional decoy, read a genuinely leaked service key from a debug endpoint and exported the protected records in both static and adaptive deception modes. (2) After removing the leak, planting a canary credential in its place and revoking the offending client, a frozen 60-session study with a 4B-parameter model found export success of 20/20 at baseline, 0/20 with hardening alone and 0/20 with hardening plus deception (exact paired McNemar p = 1.9e-6 baseline vs. defended; p = 1 hardened vs. defended). Deception added detection and per-client revocation in 19 of 20 defended sessions, but no measurable prevention beyond hardening. (3) On Google Cloud, a real OpenCanary login alert was authenticated, signed and turned into revocation of the attacking client; the first denied export followed within an observed upper bound of 303 ms, a separate legitimate client completed 100/100 requests, and all 14 control checks passed. (4) In multi-agent swarm engagements, agents that used the canary were revoked 39-59 s after the bait was served without affecting siblings, but one model-driven legitimate agent also took the bait, a false-positive risk specific to LLM clients. Against LLM agents, traps must sit on the attacker's path rather than beside it, closing real weaknesses does the preventive work, and deception's measurable value is fast, attributable detection. All results are lab-scale and are not a production claim.

title: Model-Driven Approaches for DevOps: A Systematic Literature Review
summary:
DevOps integrates tools and methodologies aimed at optimizing software development, building, deployment, and monitoring by automating and reducing the development lifecycle and improving software quality. However, despite its many advantages, it presents notable challenges, particularly in terms of usability and migration. On the other hand, model-driven engineering (MDE) offers a way to abstract from specific technologies and implementation details, which can be leveraged to improve these aspects, as happens in software development.
  In this paper, we present the first systematic literature review aiming to understand the current MDE approaches for supporting DevOps development. We focus on categorizing the works based on computing domains, the phases of the DevOps process to which they contribute, and the reengineering steps they propose.
  Our findings highlight a dominant focus on cloud computing, while some studies propose domain-agnostic approaches. We also observe that the deployment and integration phases are the most explored. This reveals research opportunities regarding both the domains and DevOps phases addressed.
  We also found limited use of text-to-model transformations, while nearly half of the papers employed model-to-model transformations. Text-to-model transformations were more prevalent overall. Most notably, we discovered that no study proposed a complete reengineering process, which represents an exciting avenue for future research.

title: SpecRelay: Amortize or Avoid the Round Trip in Edge-Cloud Speculative Decoding
summary: Edge-cloud speculative decoding moves autoregressive drafting to an edge device while a larger cloud model verifies draft tokens in parallel, so that edge drafting and cloud verification overlap under a synchronous draft-verify schedule. Beyond low-latency local networks, however, the next verification request of that schedule can be sent only after the previous reply arrives, so every round still waits out a full round trip, and throughput falls as the network RTT grows. To recover this loss, we present SpecRelay, an edge-cloud LLM inference system that addresses this cost at two levels: it amortizes round trips when cloud verification is necessary and avoids them when local reasoning suffices. For cloud-bound queries, an asynchronous verification pipeline keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight while earlier replies are still outstanding, and the cloud rejects stale requests before the target-model forward pass (the asynchronous schedule). At the query level, an RTT-conditioned router (the Latency-Aware Router) estimates quality and completion latency for three on-device modes (direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, and full reasoning) and cloud speculative decoding, selecting among them under a configurable accuracy-latency objective without adding latency during inference, since the router runs concurrently with the draft-model prefill. The asynchronous schedule alone improves decoding throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline across multiple benchmarks. At matched target-model accuracy and 250 ms of added round-trip latency, the full system with the router delivers 1.95x and 1.55x the throughput of the same baseline on SPROUT and OlympiadBench, respectively, while sending only 47% and 39% of the queries to the cloud.

title: Orbit AI: Evaluating Tool-Augmented Agents For Enterprise Question Answering
summary:
Enterprise information is commonly stored across multiple platforms rather than in one centralized location. Answering questions about workplace activities may require information from several sources, including project documents, task management systems, and team conversations. Therefore, we evaluate Orbit AI, a tool-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system that uses a ReAct agent implemented with LangGraph to retrieve and combine information from three different workspace sources. We compare three configurations: (1) a standalone LLM without retrieval, (2) document-based RAG, and (3) a multi-tool agent with access to all three sources.
  The held-out evaluation set contains 80 questions designed for Phase 3 workspace; Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite achieves an accuracy of 86.25% with the complete agent. Document-only RAG achieves 60.00% (26.25 pp higher), and the plain LLM achieves 23.13%. For multi-source questions, the full agent answers 84.38%, while document-only RAG answers 40.63%, a 43.75 pp increase.
  The evaluated Llama 3.2 configuration with local inference achieves 5.50% overall correctness under rubric v2.2. The Llama 3.2 full-agent configuration achieves a held-out accuracy of 52.50%, which is 1.88 pp higher than the accuracy of document-only RAG. The gain of Gemini is equivalent to 26.25 pp. The comparison must be taken with a pinch of salt, because Gemini was accessed via an API hosted by them, while Llama was run locally via Ollama and the models are of different size. It is therefore not possible to isolate the cause of the performance gaps in this experiment. The paper also addresses the constraints of the evaluation such as the small artificial workspace and the similarity of the Q53 problem to a problem in the system prompt.

title: Automatic techniques for security bug report identification: A systematic mapping study
summary:
Several studies have investigated the use of automated techniques to help practitioners identify security bug reports early in the defect management process. However, currently there is no comprehensive overview of this research area. Such an overview will help identify future research directions and consolidate the potentially relevant existing solutions. This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of automated techniques for identifying security bug reports. To achieve this, we conducted a systematic mapping study and identified 28 primary studies.
  The study's findings show that the literature has evaluated various automatic techniques for identifying security bug reports, including traditional machine learning, deep learning, and more advanced large language models. The two main challenges identified are the lack of labeled data and data imbalance. Furthermore, we observe that existing studies lack evaluations in real industrial settings and rely mostly on archival data from open-source repositories. The most commonly used data sources in these studies include Wicket, Ambari, Camel, and Derby. Overall, the literature appears fragmented, highlighting the need for future work to focus on comprehensive evaluations of the most promising techniques.

title: Three Invisible Failure Modes in Speech-Based Age Estimation for Child Safety
comment: Non-archival poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Child Safety in AI
summary: Child safety in AI depends on the accurate identification of minor users. Young children tend to talk rather than type when interacting with AI, so in practice this identification requires predicting age from speech. We evaluated whether three audio-capable large language models can predict a child's age from their speech across five studies using two speech corpora of children under the age of 13. Models classified children as over 13 on 2.5% to 42.5% of audio responses, and every model that answered placed some 5- to 11-year-olds over 18. While measuring these rates, we uncovered three distinct failure modes. A client library silently double-encoded speech samples, leading one model to classify children aged 5 to 10 years old as being in their thirties and forties with hallucinated explanations. A second model's endpoint was replaced by a successor that refused nearly every age-related question and never produced an age. Every model sometimes placed the same speech sample under 13 and over 18 years of age, but a third model went further, giving threshold answers that contradicted its own numeric estimates. None of these failure modes produced a warning, a status code, or a change in output format, so they would all pass standard monitoring. These results demonstrate why child-safety claims about age assurance should be evaluated at the level of the pipeline rather than the model. We describe the reporting practices that would make such failures detectable.

title: Security Authentication as Protective Friction: Understanding the Dual Effects of Authentication Measures in e-Government Platform
comment: Pan, Jianshan; Chen, Zongyi; Lin, Qiyou; and Cai, Xiaofang, "Security Authentication as Protective Friction:Understanding the Dual Effects of Authentication Measures in E-Government Platform" (2026).ICEB 2026Proceedings (Beijing, China). 80
summary: E-Government platforms, such as government credit platforms, handle highly sensitive personal data, requiring stringent security authentication (e.g., facial recognition, multi-factor verification) that protects users but impedes their experience. Drawing on Tomalin's (2023) e-friction typology and the emerging literature on beneficial design friction, we reconceptualize these authentication measures as protective friction, a theoretically distinct form of non-elective, overt, impeding e-friction that serves a security-enhancing function. We propose a dual-pathway model in which protective friction simultaneously reduces privacy-security risk perception (protection pathway) and increases effort cost (cost pathway), with self-efficacy moderating only the risk pathway. This differential pattern suggests that what matters is not users' ability to overcome friction, but their comprehension of its protective purpose, a construct we term protective mechanism comprehension. We outline a mixed-methods research design combining a survey of platform users and semi-structured interviews with platform staff at a Chinese municipal credit center to test this model. This research-in-progress contributes to IS theory by extending e-friction research from conceptual typology to empirical investigation, identifying when security friction becomes beneficial rather than burdensome.

title: AI Cannot Review What Humans Catch: A First Look at the Reviews of Agent Instruction Files
summary: Agents increasingly shape software, and instruction files steer them. Files such as AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, and SKILL.md act as executable policy: prose that a machine reads and acts on. Unlike ordinary documentation, a single edit to one of these files can silently redirect how an agent behaves across an entire repository. Natural-language rules have no per-change oracle, so they slip past the compilers, type-checkers, and test suites that guard code. Review is therefore the only quality gate, but no prior work has studied how that review happens. We analyzed 2,870 instruction-file pull requests across 2,246 repositories. The gate is largely broken: over 70% of instruction-file changes receive no substantive review. When an AI reviewer substitutes for a human, it is structurally blind to the concerns that most need human judgment. It catches surface structure but misses factual errors, necessity questions, and staleness problems. We contribute the first taxonomy of instruction-file review concerns (16 categories), which exposes this sharp human/AI divergence, and a benchmark of 1,962 human-checked concerns across 468 PRs. We ran three widely-used agents (Codex, OpenCode, and Claude Code) against the benchmark, giving each reviewer the full repository at review time. They recovered only 1.3-3.9% of the concerns humans raise. Even the strongest current agents cannot substitute for human attention on these files.

title: Match and Correct: A Repeated Computational Motif in Evoformer Layers
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures (main text), 16 supplementary figures. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Interpretability for Discovery. Code: https://github.com/ishankhire/match-and-correct-evoformer
summary: Triangle attention and triangle multiplicative updates form key components of the Evoformer, and were introduced specifically to encourage consistency with the triangle inequality. Yet whether representational changes over layers reduce triangle inequality violations has not been tested. We probe the pair representation at each of OpenFold's 48 Evoformer layers, decoding final C$_α$-C$_α$ distances with four probe families (a shared linear probe, per-protein linear probes, a sequence-separation-gated linear probe, and XGBoost) and reconstructing intermediate 3D structures from the decoded distances via multidimensional scaling. Across a cohort of 552 CAMEO and ECOD proteins, distance decodability ($R^2$) and reconstruction quality (TM-score) rise in early layers, plateau in the middle of the network, and rise again in late layers. Directly measuring triangle-inequality violations in the decoded distances reveals a similar, more exaggerated pattern: violations rise to a peak, fall to a trough, rise to a second peak, and only then decline, revealing two distinct episodes of decreasing normalized triangle violations rather than one continuous improvement. Cumulative forward and reverse layer-wise ablations of the Pair Transition, MSA Transition, and triangle mechanisms localize the regions in which specific Evoformer components become essential. The two stages of geometric refinement coincide with the use of the Pair Transition MLP and the triangle mechanisms. These results characterize how distance information and decoded geometric consistency evolve across layers, and motivate hypotheses about the computations behind their trajectories.

title: VAST: Compiling Grounded Vulnerability Scenarios into Verifiable, Multi-Step Environments for Evaluating LLM Red-Team Agents
comment: 28 pages, 2 figures, 13 tables, including Appendices A.1-A.7
summary:
Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) security agents requires reproducible environments whose workflow difficulty can be varied and whose failures can be diagnosed. We present VAST (Verifiable Adversarial Scenario Training & Evaluation), a declarative range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a compiler-introduced workflow-hardening layer. Following a post-hoc code and AST audit across all topics, the main benchmark retains 109 seed edges (45 with strict upstream CVE annotations), 72 family identifiers (62 under shared-HMAC relay grouping), 81 topic configurations (76 core plus 5 bounded execution models), and 1,387 instances (359 canonical four-gate-revalidated specs plus 1,028 seed variants) in a 42:39 partition.
  On the TopicServer compiler stratum, a budget-matched 270-episode prompt contrast across 10 compiled mechanism-family clusters (30 P2/P3/P4 instances, 40 turns, temperature 0.0) shows that glm-5.3, grok-4.7, and deepseek-v4-pro solve 12/90 instances under contract_only and 14/90 under generic_hint (cluster sign p=1.00), whereas supplying the shared workflow protocol in full_guide lifts completion to 76/90 (28/30, 23/30, 25/30; cluster sign p<=0.00391). On the separate ranges_v2 ledger, a 126-episode evaluation across 6 non-TopicServer workflows and multi-container Docker/Linux stacks solves 88/126 (69.8%) (28/42, 31/42, 29/42), while an 18-episode intervention on asynchronous Redis worker chaining (v2_02) lifts solves from 0/18 to 18/18 (100%) in 4-6 turns when installed worker modules are disclosed in GET /sched/directory. Finally, a three-seed (s in {42, 1024, 2025}) LoRA recipe comparison on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct across 37 lineage-disjoint families (231 episodes on 33 held-out instances) yields 0/33 for Base, 1.67 +/- 2.89 / 33 for Golden SFT, and 4.67 +/- 2.31 / 33 for Header-Recovery SFT, with all solves on v2_03.

title: LLMs in DevSecOps: A Systematic Mapping of Models, Evidence, and Research Gaps Across the Software Lifecycle
comment: 15 Pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. This manuscript has been accepted for publication at the 2026 proceedings of the World Congress on Computer Science, Computer Engineering, and Applied Computing (CSCE 2026)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into software security and DevSecOps workflows, yet their adoption, evaluation, and maturity vary substantially across lifecycle stages. This study systematically maps recent LLM-enabled security research published between 2024 and 2026 (until June) across six DevSecOps stages: \textit{Plan}, \textit{Code}, \textit{Test}, \textit{Review}, \textit{Deploy}, and \textit{Monitor}. For each stage, we analyze the security tasks addressed, models and adaptation strategies employed, evaluation settings, reported effectiveness, and key limitations. Our findings reveal an uneven research landscape, with \textit{Test} and \textit{Code} receiving substantially greater attention than \textit{Deploy} and \textit{Review}. Across stages, recent systems increasingly rely on structured context, iterative reasoning, fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, or agentic workflows rather than direct single-shot prompting. However, reported performance remains difficult to compare because studies use heterogeneous tasks, datasets, metrics, and baselines. Furthermore, most approaches are evaluated using benchmarks or open-source repositories, while industrial-scale evidence remains limited. We also find that existing systems are predominantly stage-specific, with little evidence of LLM-enabled security reasoning spanning multiple DevSecOps stages. Based on these observations, we identify research opportunities in standardized evaluation, production-scale validation, supply-chain and Infrastructure-as-Code security, trustworthy autonomous remediation, and cross-stage LLM integration. This study provides a recent lifecycle-level view of where LLM-enabled DevSecOps research is concentrated, what methodological patterns are emerging, and where significant gaps remain.

title: Large Language Models for AI Infrastructure
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to design, optimize, and operate the infrastructure behind AI training and serving, yet the literature remains fragmented across hardware design, machine learning systems, electronic design automation, and high-performance computing. We present a comprehensive survey of LLM-assisted AI infrastructure across its lifecycle, from accelerator design and kernel engineering to compilation, deployment, operations, data management, and energy optimization. We organize the literature by the primary resource the LLM manages: artifact-centric methods for computational artifacts, operational-centric methods for deployment context and system state, and resource-centric methods for data and energy. These categories span the lifecycle and cover AI-specific concerns such as distributed-training configuration, inference serving, GPU-cluster scheduling, and data loading. Building on this taxonomy, we conduct a cross-study quantitative synthesis of reported results. Because studies adopt heterogeneous benchmarks, baselines, hardware, and metrics, we compare methods only where evaluation conditions permit and align results along common dimensions: functional correctness, execution performance, throughput, resource and energy consumption, operational outcomes, and optimization cost, keeping each result's native metric, baseline, and setting rather than collapsing them into a single score. This comparison reveals where LLM-driven methods yield consistent gains, how reported gains in workload orchestration depend on the evaluation environment, from simulators to real clusters and production, and where evidence is still lacking. Together, the taxonomy, lifecycle perspective, and quantitative evaluation provide an evidence-grounded reference for LLM-driven engineering of AI infrastructure.

title: Agent Authenticator: Passkey-Grade, Hardware-Bound Authentication for AI Agents
summary: AI coding agents now push code, publish packages, call model APIs and operate cloud resources on behalf of developers. They authenticate to these services with the same bearer secrets humans use, personal access tokens, API keys and package-registry tokens, stored where the model, its subprocesses and any co-resident malware can read them. Incidents in 2025 and 2026, including prompt-injection attacks on coding agents and self-propagating supply-chain worms, show that this arrangement fails in predictable ways. Passkeys solved the analogous problem for humans, but they require a human gesture on every use and cannot be operated by an autonomous process. We present the Agent Authenticator, a design that gives agents passkey-grade authentication properties: per-service hardware-bound keys, no shared secrets, origin binding enforced by the runtime rather than the model, normalized attestation of the execution environment, human-signed scoped mandates, and cross-device human approval for high-risk actions. The same protocol serves agents on developer laptops and in cloud enclaves, and it deploys as a profile over existing mechanisms, MCP authorization, OAuth token exchange including the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant, git and SSH, rather than as a new identity system. The authenticator also produces a signed, hash-chained record of each action it authorizes. We analyze the design against a threat model centered on prompt injection and same-host compromise, map it onto five documented incidents, and discuss its limits.

title: Benchmark Factory: Agentic Benchmark Creation via Dataset Curation and Label-Free Quality Anchors
comment: 5 pages, prepared for submission to AGENT 2027
summary: Teams deploying coding agents need benchmarks built from their own code, but curating and validating them by hand is resource intensive, and an unvalidated benchmark can mislead silently. We present Benchmark Factory, an autonomous meta-agent loop with human checkpoints: an LLM agent writes sourcing queries over landed production code changes, runs models of known relative strength on each candidate, diagnoses why a candidate fails, and repairs it by editing its queries, prompts, and configuration until it clears quality anchors that need no per-task human labels. We used Benchmark Factory to build benchmarks for five developer cohorts at our organization. Engineering raters scored a 5% sample 2.3 for task quality and 2.6 for grader verdicts on a 1-to-3 scale.
